topicLabel: T3.1 · Uses Python with InterSystems IRIS
title: T3.1: Uses Python with InterSystems IRIS
description: Test your knowledge of Python integration with InterSystems IRIS, including Embedded Python capabilities and selecting appropriate Python strategies for different use cases

questions.question: You are developing an IRIS class and need to add a method that uses Python machine learning libraries to analyze data stored in globals. Which keyword must you add to the method declaration to enable Embedded Python execution?

options.text: Method Analyze() As %Status [ Python ]
ClassMethod Analyze() As %Status [ Language = python ]
Method Analyze() As %Status [ Embedded = python ]
ClassMethod Analyze() As %Status [ Runtime = python ]

questions.explanation: The Language = python keyword is used to declare that a method should execute Python code instead of ObjectScript. This enables Embedded Python execution within IRIS classes. The keyword must be added to the method declaration using the square bracket syntax. Methods can be either ClassMethod or instance Method, but the keyword is always 'Language = python' not 'Python', 'Embedded', or 'Runtime'. Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=GEPYTHON_runpython

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the iris module in Embedded Python are TRUE?

options.text: The iris module provides access to IRIS globals via iris.gref()
The iris module requires a connection string to connect to IRIS
The iris module supports transaction control with iris.tstart() and iris.tcommit()
The iris module is identical to the DB-API driver module

questions.explanation: The iris module in Embedded Python provides access to globals using iris.gref() and supports transaction control with iris.tstart(), iris.tcommit(), and iris.trollback(). However, it does NOT require a connection string because Embedded Python runs in-process within the IRIS kernel. The Embedded Python iris module is different from the DB-API driver module - they have different APIs and are not interchangeable. Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=GEPYTHON_reference_core

options.text:
import iris
test = iris.cls("User.Test")
result = test.invokeMethod("bar", iris.var())

import iris
test = iris.cls("User.Test")
result = iris.bar(pResult)
print(result)

import iris
test = iris.cls("User.Test")
result = test.invokeMethod("bar")

import iris
test = iris.cls("User.Test")
byref = iris.ref(None)
test.bar(byref)
result = byref.value

questions.explanation: When calling ObjectScript methods with ByRef parameters from Embedded Python, you must use iris.ref() to create a reference object that can be modified by the method. The iris.ref(None) creates a reference initialized to None, which is passed to the method. After the method executes, byref.value contains the result. Options a and c don't properly handle the ByRef parameter, and option b incorrectly tries to call the method as if it were a module-level function. Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=GEPYTHON_sharedata#GEPYTHON_sharedata_passbyref

questions.question: A system administrator attempts to execute Embedded Python code in an IRIS instance but receives an IRIS_ACCESSDENIED error. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The Python runtime is not installed on the server
The %Service_CallIn service is not enabled
The user does not have %All role assigned
The iris module is not imported correctly

questions.explanation: Embedded Python requires the %Service_CallIn service to be enabled in the Management Portal. If this service is disabled, attempts to execute Embedded Python code will fail with an IRIS_ACCESSDENIED error. While Python runtime installation and proper user permissions are important, the specific IRIS_ACCESSDENIED error in the context of Embedded Python typically indicates that %Service_CallIn is disabled. Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=GEPYTHON_prereqs

questions.question: Which of the following capabilities are available ONLY with Embedded Python and NOT with DB-API or pyODBC?

options.text: Creating SQL stored procedures and functions in Python
Connecting to IRIS from external Python applications
Augmenting existing IRIS classes with Python methods
Executing SQL SELECT statements

questions.explanation: Embedded Python uniquely supports creating SQL stored procedures, functions, and triggers in Python, as well as augmenting existing IRIS classes with Python methods using the Language = python keyword. DB-API and pyODBC are designed for external client applications to connect to IRIS, which Embedded Python does not do (it runs in-process). All Python options support executing SQL statements. Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=AFL_epython

questions.question: Your team is building a Flask web application that will query IRIS patient data and display it in a dashboard. The application will run on a separate server from the IRIS instance. Which Python strategy is most appropriate?

options.text: Embedded Python - for highest performance
DB-API - for external SQL client access
Python Gateway (PEX) - for interoperability
Native API - for direct global access

questions.explanation: DB-API is the appropriate choice for external Python applications like Flask, Django, or Streamlit that need SQL access to IRIS. It provides PEP 249-compliant database connectivity over TCP/IP, making it suitable for client applications running on separate servers. Embedded Python only works in-process within IRIS (not external applications). Python Gateway is for IRIS calling external Python, not the reverse. While Native API could work, DB-API is recommended for SQL-focused external applications. Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=GPYDEV_intro_sql

questions.question: An IRIS interoperability production needs to integrate with an existing Python natural language processing service running as a separate process. IRIS must initiate calls to this Python code from business operations. Which Python integration strategy should you use?

options.text: Embedded Python - to run Python in the IRIS process
DB-API - to connect to Python from IRIS
Python Gateway (PEX) - for IRIS to call external Python
Native API - for direct global manipulation

questions.explanation: Python Gateway (PEX framework) is designed specifically for scenarios where IRIS needs to call external Python code. It inverts the control flow compared to DB-API, allowing IRIS to initiate execution of Python business services, processes, and adapters running as separate external services. This is essential for interoperability productions where IRIS orchestrates Python components. Embedded Python runs in-process (not external), and DB-API is for Python calling IRIS, not the reverse. Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=BEXTSERV

questions.question: What is the primary performance advantage of Embedded Python compared to DB-API or Native API client-server approaches?

options.text: Embedded Python uses multithreading for parallel execution
Embedded Python eliminates network latency through in-process execution
Embedded Python compiles Python code to native machine code
Embedded Python caches query results more efficiently

questions.explanation: Embedded Python's primary performance advantage is that it runs within the IRIS kernel process, eliminating network latency and serialization overhead associated with client-server approaches like DB-API and Native API. This in-process execution provides the lowest latency and tightest integration, enabling direct memory access to globals and seamless mixing of Python and ObjectScript. The performance benefit comes from eliminating inter-process communication, not from multithreading, compilation, or caching. Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=GEPYTHON

questions.question: A developer needs to access IRIS hierarchical data structures from an external Python analytics script running on the same server as IRIS. The data is stored in globals, not SQL tables. Which of the following Python options support direct global manipulation?

options.text: DB-API driver
Native API for Python
Embedded Python
pyODBC

questions.explanation: Native API and Embedded Python both support direct global manipulation. Native API provides client-server access to IRIS-specific features including global arrays from external Python processes, while Embedded Python accesses globals in-process using iris.gref(). DB-API and pyODBC only provide SQL access and cannot directly manipulate globals - they are limited to relational operations. Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=AFL_epython

questions.question: You need to create a SQL function in IRIS that uses the pandas library to perform statistical calculations on table data. Which Python strategy allows you to create SQL stored procedures and functions?

options.text: DB-API - by defining functions in external Python scripts
Embedded Python - by writing Python methods in IRIS classes
Python Gateway (PEX) - by registering Python functions
Native API - by using the iris module's SQL support

questions.explanation: Only Embedded Python supports creating SQL stored procedures, functions, and triggers. This is done by writing Python methods in IRIS classes with the Language = python keyword and appropriate SQL declarations. The Python code executes in-process with access to the pandas library and other packages. DB-API, Python Gateway, and Native API cannot create SQL stored procedures - they are designed for different use cases (external client access or interoperability). Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=RSQL_createfunction

questions.question: In Embedded Python, you need to access the %Regex.Matcher class. What are the correct syntax options to reference this class? (Select all that apply)

options.text: iris.Regex.Matcher
iris._Regex.Matcher
iris.cls('%Regex.Matcher')
iris.percent.Regex.Matcher

questions.explanation: There are two valid ways to access %Regex.Matcher in Embedded Python: (1) iris._Regex.Matcher - substitute underscores for percent signs since Python doesn't support % in identifiers; (2) iris.cls('%Regex.Matcher') - use the iris.cls() function with the full class name as a string. Options a and d use invalid syntax. Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=GEPYTHON_calliris

questions.question: When passing a Python boolean True to an ObjectScript method from Python, what value will the ObjectScript method receive?

options.text: The string 'True'
The integer 1
A %Boolean object
A Python reference object

questions.explanation: When Python booleans are passed to ObjectScript methods, they are automatically converted to integers: True becomes 1 and False becomes 0. Similarly, when ObjectScript returns boolean values to Python, they are converted to Python integers. If you need to explicitly pass Python boolean values, ObjectScript provides ##class(%SYS.Python).True() and ##class(%SYS.Python).False() methods. Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=GEPYTHON_sharedata

questions.question: You need to execute an arbitrary ObjectScript command from Embedded Python to access the $ZVERSION special variable. Which code is correct?

options.text: result = iris.$zversion
result = iris.execute('return $zversion')
result = iris.cmd('$zversion')
result = iris.objectscript.eval('$zversion')

questions.explanation: The iris.execute() function allows you to run arbitrary ObjectScript code from Python. Use 'return expr' syntax to get a value back, or just the command for side effects. For example, iris.execute('return $zversion') returns the IRIS version string, while iris.execute('write $zversion, !') would output to the terminal. This is useful for accessing ObjectScript special variables and functions that have no Python equivalent. Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=GEPYTHON_calliris

questions.question: Which statements about exception handling between Python and ObjectScript are TRUE?

options.text: Python exceptions automatically propagate to ObjectScript and can be caught in TRY-CATCH blocks
Python exceptions are wrapped as %Exception.PythonException in ObjectScript
ObjectScript $zerror is populated with the Python exception details
You must explicitly convert Python exceptions to IRIS status codes

questions.explanation: Python exceptions automatically propagate to ObjectScript and are captured in TRY-CATCH blocks. The exceptions are wrapped as %Exception.PythonException objects with the original Python error details preserved. The $zerror special variable contains the exception information. Conversion to status codes is not required - the exception mechanism handles this automatically. From Python, you can use iris.check_status() to raise ObjectScript status errors as Python exceptions. Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=GEPYTHON_sharedata

questions.question: You are writing Embedded Python code that needs to execute a SQL query against an IRIS table. Which is the correct approach?

options.text:
import pyodbc
conn = pyodbc.connect('DSN=IRIS')
cursor = conn.cursor()

sql = iris.sql.prepare('SELECT * FROM Sample.Person')
rs = sql.execute()
import intersystems_iris\nrs = intersystems_iris.query('SELECT * FROM Sample.Person')
rs = iris.execute('SELECT * FROM Sample.Person')

questions.explanation: In Embedded Python, use iris.sql.prepare() to create a prepared statement and execute() to run it. The result set is iterable and you can loop through rows directly. This approach uses the in-process connection and doesn't require external drivers like pyODBC or the DB-API driver. The iris.execute() function is for ObjectScript commands, not SQL queries. Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=GEPYTHON_calliris

questions.question: When working with binary data in ObjectScript that must be passed to Python without UTF-8 encoding, which approach should you use?

options.text: Pass the data directly as a string
Use ##class(%SYS.Python).Bytes(data) to wrap the binary data
Convert the data to base64 first
Use $ZCONVERT with 'O' mode

questions.explanation: InterSystems IRIS strings are automatically converted to UTF-8 when passed from ObjectScript to Python. For binary data that should not be converted (like image data or encrypted content), use ##class(%SYS.Python).Bytes(data) to wrap the data. This ensures the binary content is passed to Python as a bytes object without encoding conversion. Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=GEPYTHON_sharedata

questions.question: In an Embedded Python method within an IRIS class, which statements about accessing the current object are TRUE?

options.text: Use 'self' to access instance properties and methods
Use 'iris.cls(__name__)' or 'iris.ClassName' to access class methods
Instance properties are accessed as self.PropertyName
The 'this' keyword references the current object like in ObjectScript

questions.explanation: In Python methods within IRIS classes, 'self' is used to access instance properties and methods, just like standard Python. Properties are accessed as self.PropertyName. For class methods and parameters, use iris.cls(__name__) or reference the class directly as iris.ClassName. The 'this' keyword doesn't exist in Python - ObjectScript uses implicit references to the current object, but Python always requires explicit 'self'. Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=GEPYTHON_runpython

questions.question: Where does Python's standard output (print statements) go when executing Embedded Python code in an IRIS terminal session?

options.text: To the IRIS messages.log file
To a Python-specific log file
To the Terminal (console) where IRIS is running
Output is discarded unless explicitly redirected

questions.explanation: When running Embedded Python in an IRIS terminal session, Python's standard output (from print() statements) goes directly to the Terminal. However, standard error output goes to the messages.log file. This is an important distinction for debugging - print statements appear in the terminal, but error messages and stack traces may appear in the log file. Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=GEPYTHON_sharedata

questions.question: You need to create a persistent object in an IRIS class from Embedded Python and save it to the database. Given a class Sample.Person with Name property, what is the correct code?

options.text: p = iris.Sample.Person()\np.Name = 'Smith'\np.save()
p = iris.Sample.Person._New()\np.Name = 'Smith'\np._Save()
p = iris.cls('Sample.Person').new()\np.Name = 'Smith'\np.commit()
p = iris.create('Sample.Person')\np.Name = 'Smith'\niris.save(p)

questions.explanation: To create and save a persistent object from Embedded Python: use _New() to create an instance (the underscore prefix is used for IRIS methods that conflict with Python reserved words), set properties directly as attributes, and call _Save() to persist. The _Save() method returns 1 if successful. Properties behave like Python attributes, and list properties support standard operations like Insert(). Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=GEPYTHON_calliris

questions.question: An Embedded Python method needs to switch to a different namespace to access data. Which code correctly changes the namespace?

options.text: iris.namespace = 'SAMPLES'
iris.system.Process.SetNamespace('SAMPLES')
iris.execute('znspace \"SAMPLES\"')
iris.SetNamespace('SAMPLES')

questions.explanation: To switch namespaces in Embedded Python, use iris.system.Process.SetNamespace('namespacename'). This calls the %SYSTEM.Process class method to change the current namespace context. Alternatively, you could use iris.execute('znspace "SAMPLES"') to run the ObjectScript command, but the Process.SetNamespace() method is the recommended approach. The namespace property and direct SetNamespace() function don't exist at the iris module level. Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=GEPYTHON_sharedata
